outcome: Khalil, Al-Hawawsha and Al-Zoubi published a claimed proof of the invariant subspace problem for separable Hilbert spaces (a case of the stated problem for general Banach spaces) in Axioms in September 2024; Ahmed Ghatasheh's preprint, submitted November 2024 and revised March 2025, identifies a specific false step (the Fourth Claim's constructed functional is not well-defined, because the sequence in question converges weakly to zero by Bessel's inequality, contradicting what the claim requires) and the claim is refuted. The general problem, and the Hilbert-space case, remain open.
credited_humans: Khalil, Al-Hawawsha, Al-Zoubi (withdrawn claim, names as given in the Axioms paper)

disputes.summary: Khalil et al. (Axioms, Sept. 2024) claimed a full proof of the invariant subspace problem for separable Hilbert spaces. Ahmed Ghatasheh's preprint (arXiv:2411.19409, submitted Nov. 2024, revised Mar. 2025) argues the proof's 'Fourth Claim' is invalid: the functional it constructs is not well-defined because the relevant sequence must converge weakly to zero (via a complete orthonormal basis and Bessel's inequality), contradicting the nonzero weak limit the claim requires. No retraction notice from Axioms was found as of this research; secondary sources report the editorial office was 'aware of concerns' and investigating, but I could not independently confirm or date any formal retraction.

summary: The only event in the window bearing on this problem is the Khalil–Al-Hawawsha–Al-Zoubi claim (Axioms, published Sept. 2024) of a proof of the invariant subspace problem for separable Hilbert spaces, followed by Ahmed Ghatasheh's refutation (arXiv:2411.19409, Nov. 2024, revised Mar. 2025), which pinpoints a specific gap: the Fourth Claim's functional is ill-defined because the underlying sequence converges weakly to zero, contradicting the claim's requirement of a nonzero weak limit. Since the claimed proof concerned separable Hilbert spaces specifically, it would have settled a case (restriction) of the stated Banach-space problem, so per §3.1 this is in-scope; because it was withdrawn/refuted rather than accepted, status is 'progress' with an 'incident' flavor rather than 'partial' or 'resolved' — no piece of the problem was actually settled either way, so resolution_direction is null and counterexample fields are empty. I found no evidence of AI involvement anywhere in this episode: I read Ghatasheh's refutation (which thanks two named individuals for feedback, no AI credited), searched for AI/LLM connections to the invariant subspace problem broadly (Terence Tao's o1 experiments, the 'Gödel Test' paper on LLMs and easy conjectures, 'From Solvers to Research' on LLM-driven formal mathematics, and a Google DeepMind formal-conjectures GitHub issue that catalogs the problem as a formalization candidate but shows no active AI work on it), and found nothing tying any AI system to this problem's claim, refutation, or any other development in the window. The Enflo (2023, pre-window) and Neville (2023, pre-window) Hilbert-space claims remain unverified preprints per Wikipedia's live article and are outside the window in any case (first posted before 26 Jan 2024; Enflo's only revision, in April 2024, is described by the author as 'a more detailed presentation' rather than a substantive change, so it does not constitute a new event). A 2025 survey by Chalendar and Partington ('Recent perspectives on the Invariant Subspace Problem', arXiv:2507.21834) exists but I could not extract its text (PDF was returned as binary/compressed to my fetch tool); I was unable to confirm whether it reports any other post-2024 development, which is a gap in this record.
competing_reading: One could argue the Khalil et al. episode does not belong in this record at all, since it was refuted and thus never became a genuine 'case settled' — under a strict reading of §3.1, a claim that turns out to be wrong changed nothing about what a careful person would write in this bullet, so the correct status might be plain 'open' with no_change_found true, treating the claim-and-refutation as noise rather than an event. I did not take this reading because §6.1 explicitly defines 'progress' to include 'instructive failures... an AI claim announced and then withdrawn is progress' by analogy, and more directly because this is exactly the kind of dispute the instructions ask to be recorded rather than silently dropped (§7: 'A withdrawn claim is still an event').
what_would_settle_it: An official retraction or correction notice from Axioms concerning Khalil et al.'s paper, and full read access to Chalendar & Partington's 2025 survey to confirm whether it records any other post-January-2024 development on this problem that I missed.
